newsitem.title: USA: Storm pounds western U.S., disrupts power, travel.
newsitem.headline: Storm pounds western U.S., disrupts power, travel.

text.p: A powerful winter storm lashed the U.S. Northwest on Friday, cutting power to homes and businesses across Washington and Oregon as California braced for a second front that could cause flash flooding.
Snow and freezing rain fell overnight in the Seattle area, virtually shutting down the city. Major highways crossing the Cascade mountains were closed.
Puget Sound Power and Light Co., which services nine counties in western Washington state, said about 156,000 of its customers were without power on Friday.
Kristen Wappler, a spokeswoman for Puget Sound Power, said freezing rain was to blame. Tree limbs, heavy with ice, were snapping and falling on top of the power lines.

The storm stranded thousands at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airpot. The extreme conditions were causing long delays and cancellations of departing and arriving flights. Airlines canceled most departures through midday and officials urged travelers not to come to the airport at all.

In Oregon, tens of thousands of homes remained without power on Friday. About 60,000 of Portland General Electric Co's customers were still without electricity after a harsh ice storm downed local power lines on Thursday.
Rain continued to fall around Portland, but forecasters said freezing rain was not expected on Friday because temperatures had warmed.
"We won't see freezing rain any more today, but we could see some snow showers," National Weather Service forecaster Eric Boldt said from Portland.
Minor flooding was reported for some rivers and streams in northwest Oregon.

"The real concern is the number of storms that are due in over this weekend that are going to bring additional rain," said Larry Raaf, program manager with Oregon Emergency Management. "We'll be keeping our fingers crossed."

The Portland International Airport reported normal operations on Friday. Icy weather on Thursday knocked out power to the airport, forcing flight delays and cancellations that stranded some travelers overnight.
"We're still trying to catch up from yesterday. But conditions are normal," said Portland airport spokesman Darrel Buttice said.
The skies were generally calm over northern and central California, though scattered rain and snow showers were reported. A winter storm warning was in effect in the Sierra Nevada mountains.
The National Weather Service warned, however, that a second Pacific storm was bearing down on California and could reach its northern coast on Saturday.
The approaching storm could dump more than 10 inches (25 cm) of rain in some areas and cause flash flooding in northern and central California, forecasters said.
"We're trying to get people alerted in areas of potential flooding," National Weather Service forecaster Diana Henderson said from Monterey, California.
The storm, which was building north of the Hawaiian islands, could melt the snowpack in the Sierra Nevada, where residents were still digging out from the last pounding.

Last weekend, more than nine feet (3 metres) of snow fell in some parts of the popular Lake Tahoe ski resort area on the northern California-Nevada border. That blustery storm affected about 100,000 Pacific Gas & Electric Co. customers in the Sierras. Power has been restored to nearly everyone.
